selectionSummary: Three distinct world-impact developments chosen consistently for cross-border reach, civilian and economic exposure, military escalation or institutional consequences and likely lasting significance: Iran-Bahrain attacks, stalled ASEAN-China maritime rules, and drones striking shipping near Romania. This is an editorial selection, not an absolute ranking.

snapshot.summary: Bahrain said it intercepted Iranian aerial attacks as Tehran claimed a US radar strike; ASEAN and China failed to complete a South China Sea conduct code at the Manila summit; and drone strikes on commercial vessels near Romania's Sulina approaches created safety and NATO concerns.
connections: The Persian Gulf and Black Sea incidents each posed military risks to international shipping and civilians, though they occurred in separate conflicts.
ASEAN's unfinished maritime rules and Romania's requests for protection underscore difficulties securing busy sea corridors in contested regions.
Official assertions of damage, legal justification and responsibility across these stories must be distinguished from independently corroborated outcomes.
uncertainties: Independent confirmation of Iranian-claimed radar damage in Bahrain and consequences for diplomacy was unavailable.
The final content and enforcement of any ASEAN-China South China Sea conduct code remained undetermined.
Attribution and exact ship-by-ship chronology of drone incidents near Romania remained unsettled.

stories.title: Bahrain intercepts Iranian aerial attacks while Tehran claims a US radar strike
stories.summary: Bahrain issued public alerts on November 15 and said it intercepted Iranian aerial attacks. Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed to have launched six drones against US military radar at a Bahrain base, but the alleged hit remained unverified. Bahrain condemned the attacks as violations of its sovereignty, while Iran defended retaliatory force and accused Gulf states of supporting US operations. The exchange threatened fragile efforts to prevent further regional escalation.
stories.whyItMatters: Bahrain hosts key US military facilities near vital Gulf shipping routes. Retaliation can endanger civilians, expand the US-Iran confrontation and undermine negotiations important to regional energy trade.
stories.selectionRationale: Cross-border military action affecting civilian safety, US assets and major energy-shipping routes, with acute diplomatic and potential long-term regional consequences.
stories.evidenceNote: Reuters directly reports public security statements; Al Jazeera Staff contrasts rival sovereignty and self-defence explanations with reporting from Tehran; the Guardian's Rory Carroll-led synthesis (with credited agency contributions) examines broader escalation. They are separately authored originating-publisher reports, not syndicated copies. Claims of hits and legal rights are attributed.

stories.title: ASEAN-China South China Sea code remains unfinished at Manila summit
stories.summary: On November 15, Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro said ASEAN and China had not finalised a long-negotiated South China Sea code of conduct. Approximately 77–80% of the draft was agreed, but the intended legal force and geographical scope remained contested. Manila's ambition to finish the code during its chairmanship was unmet, and Singapore would inherit the effort in 2027. The absence of agreement left maritime tensions without a new regional rulebook.
stories.whyItMatters: The South China Sea supports major shipping and fishing activities, and maritime confrontations involve several sovereign states. An effective code could help prevent dangerous incidents from escalating into wider conflict.
stories.selectionRationale: Broad maritime, security and commercial consequences across several states, and the enduring institutional impact of a missed agreement deadline.
stories.evidenceNote: Reuters reported the actual Nov15 announcement; Philippine bylined reporting describes its domestic diplomatic stakes; Al Jazeera's Barnaby Lo offered separately written earlier-day analysis of negotiating barriers, not purported confirmation of the later press conference. Three different editorial owners.

commonFacts.text: ASEAN and China had not agreed a completed South China Sea code of conduct by the summit on November 15, after more than two decades of talks.
The Philippine foreign minister described about 77–80% of the draft as complete but said significant provisions remained unresolved.
The Philippines had sought to complete negotiations in 2026, while its missed goal left Singapore to pursue the deal in the next chairmanship.

framingDifferences.text: Philstar reports the missed outcome as a Philippine diplomatic promise unfulfilled; Reuters emphasises multilateral legal hurdles and disagreements inside ASEAN as well as with China.
Al Jazeera's separately reported analysis explains likely barriers before the news conference, whereas Reuters and Philstar confirm the actual November 15 no-deal outcome.

uncertainties: When negotiations might conclude and whether any code would be legally binding.
Which waters an eventual code would cover and whether it would include enforceable dispute procedures.
Whether China, the Philippines and other parties could reach concessions acceptable to their domestic constituencies.

unverifiedClaims.text: Beijing maintains its maritime conduct was lawful, while the Philippines accuses Chinese ships of aggressive actions in claimed Philippine waters.
unverifiedClaims.reason: Disputed descriptions of specific encounters are attributed; the separate 2016 arbitral ruling and China's rejection are established background.

stories.title: Romania reports drone strikes on merchant vessels near the Danube's Black Sea exit
stories.summary: Romanian authorities reported multiple drone strikes on commercial vessels near the Sulina shipping approaches on November 13–14. The ships' crews reportedly extinguished fires without fatalities. Romanian fighter jets responded and the defence minister requested more allied maritime surveillance and counter-drone equipment. The drone operator was unidentified, and the reports differed in how they counted ships across the two nights.
stories.whyItMatters: Civilian shipping near the territorial waters of a NATO member is exposed to war-related dangers on a corridor used for Ukrainian exports. Continued attacks could threaten trade, crews and regional security.
stories.selectionRationale: Internationally flagged civilian ships near an alliance member and a Ukrainian trade corridor are a cross-border humanitarian, economic and escalation risk.
stories.evidenceNote: Reuters' original Romania reporting covers NATO implications; Digi24's Romanian report details local alerts and ships; Anadolu's bylined international report groups incidents across two dates differently. Neither attribution of drone operators nor a single consistent vessel count can be independently concluded from the three.

commonFacts.text: Multiple merchant vessels near the Romanian Black Sea coast were reported struck by drones around November 13–14; Romanian authorities reported no fatalities in the incidents described.
Evia Petrol V and Marsol were among vessels reportedly hit, and crews reportedly contained fires; attribution of the drone launches was not established.
Romanian authorities reported aerial alerts and sought additional surveillance or counter-drone support; this was a request rather than confirmed new NATO deployments.

framingDifferences.text: Reuters places the maritime incidents in the context of NATO security and Ukraine's exports; Digi24 concentrates on Romanian coastal alerts, vessels and emergency response.
Anadolu combines the Friday Larissa 1 incident with two Saturday strikes, while Reuters and Digi24 use a three-ship Saturday account; the archive retains this unresolved difference.

uncertainties: Who launched each drone and whether merchant ships were the intended targets.
Whether three ships were hit on Saturday or reports grouped vessels across Friday and Saturday differently.
What future allied deployments, shipping restrictions or export impacts would follow.

unverifiedClaims.reason: Conflict-context assessment does not identify a perpetrator; no independent forensic attribution was available.

unverifiedClaims.text: Anadolu's three-vessel grouping includes Larissa 1, while other reports name Ali Najafov in the Saturday count.
